sb_prompt: WHAT ADVICE OR EXPERIENCE CAN YOU OFFER TO A PARENT ON HOW TO HELP A SON OR DAUGHTER CHOOSE A COLLEGE TO ATTEND?
raw_output:
ParticipantA: Hello!
ParticipantB: Hello!
ParticipantA: Thanks for hopping on the call. I'm looking at your profile and see we're both college grads, so I thought it would be good to chat about what we're doing now.
ParticipantB: Absolutely, I'm glad you reached out. I'm curious, how long have you been working since you finished school?
ParticipantA: Just a little over a year. I graduated in May and started my current role in July.
ParticipantB: That's exciting. What field are you in?
ParticipantA: I'm working in data analysis, mostly helping companies interpret user feedback.
ParticipantB: That sounds like a great fit. I'm in a similar vein, actually. I'm in project management, coordinating teams for software development.
ParticipantA: Oh, nice. I have a feeling I ran into a similar situation when I was helping my own brother pick a school.
ParticipantB: Really? That's interesting. My parents are in the same boat. They asked me last week if I had any advice on how to guide a child through this process, so I'm actually looking for that perspective.
ParticipantA: Oh, that's convenient. I'm in the same spot. My sister is 17 and will be applying next year, and I've been telling myself I need to figure this out better.
ParticipantB: Well, from my experience, I think the biggest thing is shifting the mindset from "what gets you in" to "what fits the student."
ParticipantA: That's a great point. I used to think the only goal was a school with a high ranking, but I realized that doesn't always mean it's the right fit.
ParticipantB: Exactly. If a student is creative but the school is purely rigorous and structured, they might burn out. I've seen kids do great at less prestigious schools because the environment matches their personality.
ParticipantA: That resonates. My sister is very introverted. I almost pushed her toward a big state university where she could just disappear in a crowd, but that would be a nightmare for her.
ParticipantB: Right, and I tell my parents the same thing. If the child is an introvert, maybe a smaller liberal arts college is better than a massive research university, even if the latter has a higher ranking.
ParticipantA: I'm starting to see that. What about the financial aspect? That's usually the biggest stressor for parents.
ParticipantB: Oh, that's huge. I always say you have to look at the net price, not just the sticker price. Sometimes a "less known" school is actually cheaper and offers better aid than the famous one.
ParticipantA: True. I actually got a scholarship I didn't expect, which made the cost manageable. But for my sister, we're worried about debt.
ParticipantB: That's why I tell parents to use the FAFSA early and look at "value" metrics. You want a school where the graduate debt is manageable relative to the starting salary.
ParticipantA: I like that approach. It takes the emotion out of the decision and focuses on the math. Do you think they should visit campuses?
ParticipantB: I definitely think so. There's no substitute for walking around. Sitting in a lecture hall for a day can tell you a lot about the vibe.
ParticipantA: My sister wants to visit, but she's nervous about talking to strangers. How do you handle that?
ParticipantB: I suggest visiting on a weekend when there are no tours scheduled, just walking around the library and the dining hall. It feels less pressured. Also, try to talk to current students, not just admissions staff.
ParticipantA: Good tip. That makes sense. She might be more comfortable asking a sophomore in the cafeteria than an admissions officer.
ParticipantB: Exactly. Current students are honest. They'll tell you what they hate about the food or the professors, which is crucial info.
ParticipantA: I should definitely encourage her to talk to current students. What about the majors? Do parents need to be experts in that?
ParticipantB: Not at all. In fact, it can be counterproductive. Parents often know more about a field than their kids, which can be intimidating.
ParticipantA: That's true. My sister wants to study psychology, but my parents think she should be an engineer because it pays more.
ParticipantB: That's a classic conflict. My advice to them is to listen to the kid's genuine interest. If they love the subject, they will stick with it even if it's harder. Passion is a great driver.
ParticipantA: I think that's hard to argue. If she hates it, she won't make it through the four years.
ParticipantB: Right. Also, check if the major is available at the school. Some smaller colleges only offer general psychology, not specialized tracks, which might limit her future options.
ParticipantA: That's a good practical point. I'll check their catalog for her specific interests. What else do you think is important?
ParticipantB: Location. Do you think they should consider living at home to save money?
ParticipantA: I think that's a gray area. For my sister, living at home might be good for money, but she needs to learn independence.
ParticipantB: Yes, that's a key one. Living away from home is a rite of passage. It forces them to manage their time and budget.
ParticipantA: I agree. My brother actually hated living with us because we were always telling him what to do. He learned a lot from living in a dorm, even if it was stressful.
ParticipantB: Exactly. If the school is far enough away that they have to live on campus or rent an apartment, that's a huge benefit for their growth.
ParticipantA: That makes sense. I didn't realize how much that factor matters. What about safety?
ParticipantB: Safety is huge. Parents always worry about this. I tell them to look up crime statistics, but also to visit and get a feel for the neighborhood.
ParticipantA: Is that easy to do?
ParticipantB: It can be tricky. Some schools don't publish specific data. I suggest looking at the "Safe College" list and asking the school directly about their policies on campus safety.
ParticipantA: I'll definitely look into that. It's reassuring to have a checklist like that. Do you think they should prioritize a school they already have a scholarship for?
ParticipantB: Often, yes. But not always. If the scholarship is from a specific program that isn't a good fit for the student, it might be better to take a loan at a school that matches their career goals better.
ParticipantA: That's a tough balance. I feel like if she has to take a huge loan just to go to the "right" school, that might kill the motivation.
ParticipantB: That's the dilemma. I tell parents to calculate the debt-to-income ratio again. If the loan is 50% of her expected first-year salary, that's usually fine. If it's 150%, that's a red flag.
ParticipantA: Okay, that gives us a concrete number to work with. I'll run the numbers on the top three schools she likes.
ParticipantB: Good idea. Also, make sure she knows she can change her mind. The first choice doesn't have to be the only choice.
ParticipantA: That's a relief. My parents are really set on her getting into the top 20 national schools. I'm trying to convince them it's okay to apply to a state school as a backup.
ParticipantB: That's the best advice I can give. If they only apply to Ivy League schools and don't get in, the student will feel crushed. They need a realistic list.
ParticipantA: I will definitely emphasize that with my parents. A safety school is essential.
ParticipantB: Absolutely. And remember, the student is the one attending, not the parent. They need to buy in emotionally.
ParticipantA: Right. If I push too hard, she might just do it for me and not herself.
ParticipantB: Exactly. You want her to feel like *she* chose this path, even if you helped map it out.
ParticipantA: That's a good way to frame it. "We" chose this together, rather than "You" chose this because I said so.
ParticipantB: Precisely. It builds confidence. What else? How about the application process itself?
ParticipantA: That's stressful. Do you think they need to start the essays early?
ParticipantB: Yes, definitely. The essays are personal and take time to write. Don't wait until the deadline.
ParticipantA: I'll tell her to start brainstorming immediately. What about letters of recommendation?
ParticipantB: Teachers and counselors know them well. I suggest asking teachers who know the student best, not necessarily the ones with the highest grades.
ParticipantA: Good point. My sister is an A-student, but she excels more in art than in math. Maybe I should ask her art teacher?
ParticipantB: Yes! If the student is going to art school, a math teacher won't be able to vouch for their potential in the right way.
ParticipantA: I never thought of that. I was thinking just the principal's office.
ParticipantB: That's a common mistake. Get recommendations that highlight specific talents relevant to the major.
ParticipantA: I'll make sure she talks to her art teacher about her portfolio. Anything else?
ParticipantB: Well, budgeting for the application fees. They can be expensive.
ParticipantA: Oh, I forgot about that. There's a fee for every school.
ParticipantB: Yes. Some schools offer fee waivers for low-income students, so check that first. It can save hundreds of dollars.
ParticipantA: That's a great tip. I'll check if she qualifies for those waivers before she starts applying.
ParticipantB: Perfect. And finally, don't forget to celebrate the end of the process. It's a long journey.
ParticipantA: Yes, they will need support. It's a big emotional rollercoaster.
ParticipantB: Exactly. Whether they get in or not, the work they put in deserves recognition.
ParticipantA: I really appreciate this conversation. You gave me a lot of practical steps to talk to my parents.
ParticipantB: It was my pleasure. I'm glad I could offer some perspective. I think it helps to have a second opinion on these things.
ParticipantA: Definitely. I feel much more prepared now. Thanks for the advice on the net price and the student voice.
ParticipantB: You're welcome. Good luck helping your sister navigate this.
ParticipantA: Thanks. I'll keep you posted on how it goes.
ParticipantB: Sounds good. All the best.
ParticipantA: Goodbye!
ParticipantB: Goodbye!
